concepts.title: Concept of Self: Personal and Social Identity

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Concept of Self: Personal and Social Identity' refers to.
questions.a: The self is the whole set of conscious ideas, thoughts and feelings a person holds about her or his own existence; it splits into a personal identity that marks one off from everybody else and a social identity that ties one to a group, and it works both as the knower (subject) and the known (object).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Concept of Self: Personal and Social Identity'.
questions.a: A newborn has no self - it takes shape through interaction with parents, friends and teachers, and it keeps changing with experience.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Concept of Self: Personal and Social Identity', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: self = personal_identity + social_identity ; subject_knower plus object_known

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Self-esteem, Self-efficacy and Self-regulation' refers to.
questions.a: Self-esteem is the value judgment a person passes on her or his own worth; self-efficacy is the belief that one personally controls life outcomes rather than luck or fate; and self-regulation is the capacity to organise, monitor and restrain one's own behaviour, including delaying gratification.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Self-esteem, Self-efficacy and Self-regulation'.
questions.a: By age 6-7 children judge themselves in four areas - academic, social, physical-athletic and appearance - and warm, accepting parenting raises esteem while over-assisting parents lower it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Self-esteem, Self-efficacy and Self-regulation', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: self_esteem = own_worth_judgment ; self_efficacy = perceived_personal_control ; self_regulation = organised_monitored_behaviour

concepts.title: Culture and Self: Indian versus Western Views

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Culture and Self: Indian versus Western Views' refers to.
questions.a: Western culture draws a comparatively fixed line between self and others, keeping individual and group as separate entities, whereas the Indian view lets that line shift - the self sometimes fuses with the cosmos or the group and at other times turns wholly inward.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Culture and Self: Indian versus Western Views'.
questions.a: Individualistic Western cultures hold self and group apart, while collectivistic Asian cultures keep the self in harmonious co-existence with its group.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Culture and Self: Indian versus Western Views', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: western_self = fixed_self_other_boundary ; indian_self = shifting_boundary_with_cosmos_and_group

concepts.title: Type and Trait Approaches to Personality

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Type and Trait Approaches to Personality' refers to.
questions.a: Type approaches sort people into broad behavioural patterns - Hippocrates' four humours, Charak Samhita's tridosha and trigunas, Sheldon's body builds, Jung's introvert-extravert, and Friedman and Rosenman's Type-A and Type-B - while trait approaches such as Allport's cardinal-central-secondary scheme, Cattell's sixteen source traits and Eysenck's dimensions rate people on specific attributes along which they differ consistently.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Type and Trait Approaches to Personality'.
questions.a: Types are simple and stereotype-prone; traits are relatively stable over time, fairly consistent across situations, and their combinations create individual differences.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Type and Trait Approaches to Personality', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: type_approach = broad_behavioural_patterns ; trait_approach = specific_enduring_attributes

concepts.title: Freud: Structure of Personality and Defence Mechanisms

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Freud: Structure of Personality and Defence Mechanisms' refers to.
questions.a: Freud pictures the mind as three levels of consciousness - conscious, preconscious and unconscious - and personality as a contest among id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle) and superego (moral branch); when the ego cannot bear anxiety it distorts reality through defence mechanisms such as repression, projection, denial, reaction formation and rationalisation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Freud: Structure of Personality and Defence Mechanisms'.
questions.a: The libido energises the id; unresolved conflict shows up in slips, jokes and dreams, and only extreme use of defences produces maladjustment.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Freud: Structure of Personality and Defence Mechanisms', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: personality_structure = id_pleasure + ego_reality + superego_moral ; defence = anxiety_reduced_by_distorting_reality

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Psychosexual Stages and Post-Freudian Theories' refers to.
questions.a: Freud places personality growth in five psychosexual stages - oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital - where failure at any stage fixes development there or pushes it back; post-Freudians widened the account: Jung's collective unconscious of archetypes, Horney's basic anxiety from disturbed childhood relations, Adler's inferiority complex and individual psychology, Fromm's social orientation, and Erikson's lifelong search for ego identity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Psychosexual Stages and Post-Freudian Theories'.
questions.a: The Oedipus complex is resolved in the phallic stage by identifying with the same-sex parent; neo-analytic theorists trimmed sexuality and enlarged the ego and social forces.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Psychosexual Stages and Post-Freudian Theories', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: stages = oral + anal + phallic + latency + genital ; fixation_or_regression = unresolved_stage_conflict

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Humanistic, Behavioural and Cultural Approaches' refers to.
questions.a: Behaviourists treat personality as reinforced stimulus-response learning where the response is the structural unit; the cultural approach reads personality as adaptation to a group's economic maintenance system, as the Birhor hunting-gathering and agricultural contrasts show; and humanists - Rogers with the real and ideal self plus unconditional positive regard, Maslow with self-actualisation at the top of the needs hierarchy - see people striving to fulfil their potential.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Humanistic, Behavioural and Cultural Approaches'.
questions.a: A gap between real and ideal self breeds unhappiness; children of hunting-gathering societies learn independence and achievement while agricultural socialisation rewards obedience and nurturance.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Humanistic, Behavioural and Cultural Approaches', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: rogers_congruence = real_self matches ideal_self -> fully_functioning_person ; maslow_top_need = self_actualisation

questions.q: How many statements does the MMPI contain and how is it divided for diagnosis? Use the method 'Self-Report Measures and Rating-Scale Scoring'. Work with: academic_rating = 500, appearance_rating = 150, area_count = 500, physical_rating = 5, social_rating = 12. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of esteem_mean.
questions.a: 1.334 units

questions.q: Compute the average rating from a four-area self-esteem checklist with given marks. Use the method 'Self-Report Measures and Rating-Scale Scoring'. Work with: academic_rating = 20, appearance_rating = 40, area_count = 250, physical_rating = 25, social_rating = 45. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of esteem_mean.
questions.a: 0.52 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Self-Report Measures and Rating-Scale Scoring' refers to.
questions.a: Self-report measures are structured questionnaires - MMPI with 567 true-false statements on 10 subscales, Eysenck's EPQ, Cattell's 16PF - where responses are scored quantitatively and read against norms; their weak points are social desirability and acquiescence, the habit of agreeing with items regardless of content.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Self-Report Measures and Rating-Scale Scoring'.
questions.a: Average the ratings a person gives across areas to quantify a self-report score; high numbers on endorsed statements mean high standing on that attribute.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Self-Report Measures and Rating-Scale Scoring', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: esteem_mean = rating_total / area_count

questions.q: Using the method 'Projective Techniques: Rorschach and TAT', work with: black_white_blots = 75, pastel_blots = 10, red_ink_blots = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of blot_total.
questions.a: 89 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Projective Techniques: Rorschach and TAT' and work with: black_white_blots = 80, pastel_blots = 80, red_ink_blots = 18. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of blot_total.
questions.a: 178 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Projective Techniques: Rorschach and TAT' refers to.
questions.a: Projective techniques reach unconscious motives through unstructured stimuli on which people project feelings and needs; shared features include ambiguous material, hidden purpose, no right or wrong answers, and subjective lengthy scoring; the Rorschach inkblot test, Thematic Apperception Test, Rosenzweig picture-frustration study, sentence completion and draw-a-person tests are the standard examples.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Projective Techniques: Rorschach and TAT'.
questions.a: The Rorschach set holds ten symmetric blots - five black and white, two with red ink, three pastel - administered in a performance proper phase and an inquiry phase.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Projective Techniques: Rorschach and TAT', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: blot_total = black_white_blots + red_ink_blots + pastel_blots
